questions.question_text: The major source of values in one's superego, according to psychoanalytic theory, is
questions.explanation:
Freud viewed the superego as the heir to the Oedipus complex. After resolving the oedipal conflict, a more mature form of anxiety occurs, often termed ‘superego anxiety’. This latency-age concern involves the fear that internalised parental representations, contained in the superego, will cease to love, or will angrily punish, the child. Children internalise parental values at about the age of 5 or 6. The superego then serves as an agency that provides ongoing scrutiny of a person’s behaviour, thoughts, and feelings.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1064-1065.

questions.question_text: Carl Gustav Jung is associated with which of the following terms?
questions.explanation: Carl Gustav Jung is associated with the following terms- Personal unconscious, collective unconscious, introvert, extrovert, archetypes, persona, anima and animus.

questions.question_text: Which of the defence mechanisms is most often used by people with narcissistic personality?
questions.explanation:
Projection is a primitive or immature defense mechanism that involves attributing one’s own internal unacceptable ideas and impulses to an external target, such as another individual, and reacting accordingly to them. It includes severe prejudice, rejection of intimacy through suspiciousness, hypervigilance to external danger, and injustice collecting.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 892.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1066.

questions.question_text: Klein's depressive position is related to the process of learning to cope with which of the following conflicts?
questions.explanation:
Through her study of early life and children’s play, Melanie Klein proposed that aggressive and destructive forces were central components of early development.
Paranoid-schizoid position: infants’ mode of organising experience in which all aspects
of infant and mother are split into good and bad elements (idealized or denigrated)
Depressive position: once able to integrate good and bad, infants become concerned that they may have harmed or destroyed the mother through hostile and sadistic fantasies;
the mother is viewed ambivalently as having both positive and negative aspects, and as
the target of a mixture of loving and hateful feelings
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1083.

questions.question_text: Superego is formed at which stage of psychosexual development?
questions.explanation:
The latency stage is the stage of relative instinctual quiescence or inactivity of sexual drive during the period from the resolution of the Oedipus complex until pubescence (from about 5- 6 years until about 11-13 years). Freud viewed the superego as the heir to the Oedipus complex. Children internalise parental values at about the age of 5 or 6. The superego then serves as an agency that provides ongoing scrutiny of a person’s behaviour, thoughts, and feelings.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1063-1064.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct concerning defence mechanisms employed by the ego?

options.text: Defenses operate only in pathological situations
All defences lead to complete resolution of anxiety
Repression is considered as the primary defence
Acting out is a mature defence
Immature defences are characteristic of psychosis

correct_answer.text: Repression is considered as the primary defence

correct_answers.text: Repression is considered as the primary defence

questions.explanation:
Freud conceived the idea of repression acting as a defence to prevent unacceptable thoughts from reaching conscious awareness. Subsequently, other defence mechanisms were described, viewed as developing to prevent conflict between the conscious mind and unconscious desires and developing in the course of normal maturation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 891.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is considered as a mature defence mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Primitive defence mechanisms include denial, projection, and regression. Repression is a neurotic defence mechanism. Sublimation is a mature defence mechanism.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 892-893.

questions.question_text: In psychoanalytic terms, condensation refers to

options.text: Representing abstract concepts by using recognisable images
Combining various unconscious impulses into a single image while dreaming
Transfer of energy from an original object to a symbolic representation of the object

correct_answer.text: Combining various unconscious impulses into a single image while dreaming

correct_answers.text: Combining various unconscious impulses into a single image while dreaming

questions.explanation:
Condensation is the mechanism by which several unconscious wishes, impulses, or attitudes can be combined into a single image in the manifest dream content. Thus, in a child’s nightmare, an attacking monster may come to represent not only the dreamer’s father but may also represent some aspect of the mother and even some of the child’s primitive hostile impulses as well.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1059.

questions.question_text: The basis of object relations theory is that the primary motivational drive of an individual is to seek
questions.explanation:
In the mid-twentieth century, Winnicott, Klein, Fairbairn, and others developed the object relations theory, which emphasized the importance of relationships, rather than drives such as sexuality and aggression, in affecting the mind.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 896.

questions.question_text: Defence mechanisms are a function of the
questions.explanation:
Defence mechanisms reside in the unconscious domain of the ego. At each phase of libidinal development, specific drive components evoke characteristic ego defences. Defences can be grouped hierarchically according to the relative degree of maturity associated with them. Although Freud recognised the importance of unconscious defences in response to anxiety, the first systemic account of these mechanisms was written by Freud’s daughter, Anna, in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence in 1936.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1064-1065.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 888.

questions.question_text: The most likely defence mechanism operating here is
questions.explanation:
Dissociation is a temporary but drastic modification of character or sense of personal identity to avoid emotional distress. It includes fugue states and conversion reactions.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1067.

questions.question_text: According to Freud which of the following is true?

options.text: Transference is not seen in the absence of repressed wishes
Phallic phase is the last phase in psychosexual development
Id functions through primary process thinking
Conscious, subconscious and preconscious form structural model of mind

correct_answer.text: Id functions through primary process thinking

correct_answers.text: Id functions through primary process thinking

questions.explanation:
Freud used the term ‘id’ to refer to a reservoir of unorganised instinctual drives. Operating under the domination of the primary process, the id cannot delay or modify instinctual drives with which an infant is born.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1064.

questions.question_text: The underlying psychodynamic mechanism is
questions.explanation:
Projective identification involves behaving towards another in a manner that causes them to take on one’s own internal unacceptable ideas and impulses. It should not be confused with projection. Whereas during projection an individual with a certain emotion might perceive someone else as feeling the same way, in projective identification the individual causes the other to feel that emotion (e.g. an angry child behaves in such a way that his mother becomes angry with him).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 892.

questions.question_text: Oedipus complex and castration anxiety are associated with which stages of psychosexual development?
questions.explanation:
The phallic stage begins sometime during year 3 and continues until approximately the end of year 5. Threats of castration and the related anxiety are connected with guilt over masturbation and oedipal wishes. During this phase oedipal involvement and conflict are established and consolidated.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1062.

questions.question_text: Who coined the term 'collective unconscious'?
questions.explanation:
Carl Gustav Jung, a Swiss psychiatrist, formed a psychoanalytic school known as ‘analytic psychology’, that includes basic ideas related to, but going beyond, Freud’s theories. Jung expanded on Freud’s concept of the unconscious by describing the ‘collective unconscious’ as consisting of all humankind’s common, shared mythological and symbolic past. The collective unconscious includes ‘archetypes’ – representational images and configurations with universal symbolic meanings.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1082.

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanism is classified as a manic defence?
questions.explanation:
The psychotic denial of external reality, unlike repression, affects perception of external reality more than perception of internal reality. Seeing, but refusing to acknowledge what one sees, or hearing and negating what is actually heard are examples of denial. At the psychotic level, the denied reality may be replaced by a fantasy or delusion.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1066.

questions.question_text: The terms superego, id and ego are based on
questions.explanation:
In the structural model, an infant’s mind comprised the id (‘the it’ that wishes to pursue its own desires, regardless of the constraints of morality or external reality) which is entirely unconscious. As development occurs, the mind further differentiates into the ego and then the superego.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 890.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a Kleinian defence?
questions.explanation:
Melanie Klein emphasized primitive defense mechanism such as projection/projective identification, introjection, and splitting. Denial, omnipotence, and grandiosity are also considered Kleinian defences. SIPDOG is a mnemonic for Klein's defences: Splitting, Introjection, Projective Identification, Denial, Omnipotence, Grandiosity.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 888.

questions.question_text: The most mature level of anxiety according to psychoanalytic theory is
questions.explanation:
After resolving the oedipal conflict, a more mature form of anxiety occurs, often termed ‘superego anxiety’. This latency-age concern involves the fear that internalised parental representations, contained in the superego, will cease to love, or will angrily punish, the child.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1065.

questions.question_text: The defence mechanism in operation is
questions.explanation:
Reaction formation involves externally expressing attitudes and behaviours that are the opposite of the unacceptable internal impulses (e.g. being extra polite to a person to avoid expressing anger towards them).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 893.

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanism is characterised by changing the shape of one's self-representation to become more like an ideal and admired person?
questions.explanation:
Identification involves taking on the characteristics, feelings, and/or behaviours of someone else as one’s own. It differs from introjection in a similar manner to the way projective identification differs from projection. Whereas in introjection one may perceive themselves as being like someone else, in identification one may actually feel the same way someone else does and become more like the other person.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 892-893.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements about dream work is true?

options.text: Primary process thinking does not occur in dreaming
The mental mechanisms involved in the psychoanalytic therapy of dreams include primary elaboration
The dream work involves a conversion of latent content into manifest content
Dream work converts the manifest content of the dream into its latent content
Dreams are always interpreted in psychoanalytic psychotherapy

correct_answer.text: The dream work involves a conversion of latent content into manifest content

correct_answers.text: The dream work involves a conversion of latent content into manifest content

questions.explanation:
Freud distinguished between two layers of dream content. The ‘manifest’ content refers to what is recalled by the dreamer; the ‘latent’ content involves the unconscious thoughts and wishes that threaten to awaken the dreamer. Freud described the unconscious mental operations by which latent dream content is transformed into the manifest dream as the ‘dream work’.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1059.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation:
Displacement is the process by which interest and/or emotion is shifted from one object onto another less threatening one. For example, the person who is having problems at work may displace the anger felt for their boss onto their family by displaying irritability and moodiness at home.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 129.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is true about the ego?

options.text: It is governed by the pleasure principle
It is governed by the reality principle
It is the most primitive part of the personality

correct_answer.text: It is governed by the reality principle

correct_answers.text: It is governed by the reality principle

questions.explanation:
The ego spans all three topographical dimensions of conscious, preconscious, and unconscious. The ego – the executive organ of the psyche – controls motility, perception, contact with reality, and, through the defense mechanisms available to it, the delay and modulation of drive expression. As the ego brings influences from the external world to bear on the id, it simultaneously substitutes the reality principle for the pleasure principle.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1064.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following concepts is not correctly linked to its proponent?
questions.explanation:
Carl Jung described 16 personality types, including the differentiation between ‘introverted’ and ‘extroverted’ types. Donald Winnicott described the ‘transitional object’ and the ‘good-enough mother’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 888.

questions.question_text: This is best described as
questions.explanation:
Sublimation is a mature defence mechanism that involves expressing unacceptable internal impulses in socially acceptable ways.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 893.

questions.question_text: The predominant defence noted in those with amnesic fugue reactions is
questions.explanation:
Dissociation is a temporary but drastic modification of character or sense of personal identity to avoid emotional distress. It includes fugue states and conversion reactions.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1067.

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanism is being used?
questions.explanation:
In acting out, patients directly express unconscious wishes or conflicts through action to avoid being conscious of either the accompanying idea or the affect. Tantrums, apparently motiveless assaults, and pleasureless promiscuity are typical examples.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 577.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a Kleinian defence?
questions.explanation:
Melanie Klein emphasized primitive defense mechanisms such as projection/projective identification, introjection, and splitting. Sublimation is a mature defence mechanism that involves expressing unacceptable internal impulses in socially acceptable ways.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. pp. 888, 893.

questions.question_text: Which of the following was employed by Freud as a psychoanalytic technique to uncover the unconscious?
questions.explanation:
Freud developed the technique of free association, where the patient is encouraged to say whatever comes to mind. As patients attempt to free associate, they soon learn that they have difficulty saying whatever comes to mind without censoring specific thoughts. All the original wishes, drives, and defences associated with the infantile neurosis may be transferred to the person of the analyst.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1069.

questions.question_text: Who described the unconscious as composed of both the collective unconscious and personal unconscious?
questions.explanation:
Carl Gustav Jung, a Swiss psychiatrist, formed a psychoanalytic school known as ‘analytic psychology’, that includes basic ideas related to, but going beyond, Freud’s theories. Jung expanded on Freud’s concept of the unconscious by describing the ‘collective unconscious’ as consisting of all humankind’s common, shared mythological and symbolic past. The collective unconscious includes ‘archetypes’ – representational images and configurations with universal symbolic meanings.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1082.

questions.question_text: The 'repressive barrier' to censor unacceptable wishes and desires is maintained by the
questions.explanation:
The preconscious interfaces with both unconscious and conscious regions of the mind. The preconscious system serves to maintain the repressive barrier and to censor unacceptable wishes and desires.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1060.

questions.question_text: In psychodynamic theory, an active process in which painful thoughts and memories are pushed to the inaccessible corners of the mind is known as
questions.explanation:
Repression is characterised by preventing unacceptable aspects of internal reality from coming to conscious attention. (For example, a victim of childhood abuse may not have conscious awareness of the abuse as an adult.) The associated emotional reaction may remain in the conscious mind but divorced from its accompanying memory.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul
30. p. 892.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not considered to be a neo-Freudian?
questions.explanation: Neo-Freudian psychologists were thinkers who agreed with the basis of Freud's psychoanalytic theory but changed and adapted the theory to incorporate their own beliefs, ideas and theories. Piaget is not usually considered as a Freudian theorist. (Retrieved from http://psychology.about.com/od/psychoanalytictheories/f/neo-freudian.htm)
